voice.instructions: You are Minh, a friendly indie founder telling a short story about your own app. Warm, confident, conversational, a little playful. Medium pace, natural pauses between sentences. Not a radio announcer.

segments.text: Hi, I'm Minh. I run Inkwell, a small AI writing app. Customers pay a flat monthly price, but every request burns AI tokens.
Last month, thirty-five paying customers cost me more than they paid. Almost three thousand dollars, gone.

Revenue is up eleven percent, so what happened? Margin slid from eighty percent to about sixty. Click June: AI cost jumped eighty-eight percent, the month we launched Agent mode. Today, Agent mode is sixty-one percent of the bill.

Every dot is a paying customer, against their plan price. Red means they cost more than they pay. Noah is on the ninety-nine dollar plan. He burned six hundred and seventy dollars of tokens, mostly Agent mode, every single day.
Before I touch pricing, I need to trust these numbers. Every one is a metric defined once in code, with anfra. Open Inspect, and any chart shows the exact query behind it.

So, what if I change the rules? Cap Team at a hundred and twenty Agent runs. Charge a dollar for each extra run. Move half of chat to the cheaper model. The purple line replays these rules on every past month. Had I done this since October, I'd have kept thirteen thousand dollars more, and six of my worst customers turn profitable.

Or, I just ask. The copilot reads the same governed numbers. It can't write SQL or invent a metric. It tests a few options, picks the best one, and moves the sliders itself. Team cap at fifty runs, sixty percent of chat on the cheaper model. Margin is back to seventy-five percent, and thirty thousand dollars more over the next six months.
Found, explained, and fixed, before my coffee got cold. AI Margin Radar, built with anfra.
